blocks.content: The story starts the moment a user successfully logs in.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028311-612564598.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart of the login moment: credentials verified once, a session or token issued as proof, and that proof validated on every subsequent request

blocks.content: Your server just verified the username and password. The credentials checked out. Now what? The user needs to make thousands of subsequent requests loading pages, fetching data, submitting forms. You can't ask them to send their password on every request. That would be insane.
So you issue something that proves "this request comes from someone who already authenticated." Something the client carries and presents on subsequent requests. Something the server can verify.

That something is either a session or a token. And the choice between them is not just an implementation detail it shapes your entire security model, your infrastructure requirements, your scalability strategy, and how you handle everything from logout to distributed systems.
The core question they answer differently: where does the proof of authentication live?

In session-based authentication, the proof lives on the server. The client carries only a reference to it. In token-based authentication, the proof lives in the token itself. The server carries nothing.
1. Session based authentication

When you log in, the server creates a session record and stores it. It gives you a session ID a random opaque string. You store this ID in a cookie. On every subsequent request, you send the cookie, the server looks up the session ID, finds your session data, and knows who you are.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277444488-787371216.png
blocks.alt: Sequence diagram of session-based authentication: client logs in, server creates and stores a session record, returns a session ID cookie, then looks up the session store on each request

blocks.content: The session ID is opaque it's just a random string like abc123xyz789. It reveals nothing about the user.
The actual data (user ID, roles, anything meaningful) lives on the server in the session store. The client has a key; the server has the lock and its contents.
What the session record typically contains:

session:abc123 → {

  user_id: 42,
  roles: ["admin"],
  email: "alice@example.com",
  created_at: 1704063660,
  last_active: 1704067260,
  ip_address: "203.0.113.1",
  user_agent: "Mozilla/5.0..."

}

TTL: 24 hours (rolling)

blocks.content: The server knows everything about every active session. It can see who is online, from where, doing what. It can invalidate any session instantly by deleting the Redis key.
2. Token-based authentication

When you log in, the server creates a token that contains your identity and signs it cryptographically. You store this token. On every request, you send it. The server verifies the cryptographic signature and if it's valid, trusts the claims inside without looking anything up.
The most common form is the JWT (JSON Web Token). But the principle applies to any signed token format.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277446125-760363235.png
blocks.alt: Sequence diagram of token-based authentication: client logs in, server signs a JWT and returns it, client sends the JWT in the Authorization header, server verifies the signature locally with no lookup

blocks.content: The fundamental difference: there is no server-side lookup. The server verifies a cryptographic signature a mathematical operation that requires only the public key (or shared secret for HS256). It takes microseconds. No network call to Redis. No database query. Just math.

blocks.content: The payload is base64 encoded, not encrypted. Anyone who has the token can read its contents. Never put secrets, passwords, or sensitive PII in a JWT payload. Put only what downstream services need to make decisions: user ID, roles, scopes.

The signature is what makes the token trustworthy. Only the auth server with the private key can create a valid signature. Any service with the public key can verify it. If the payload is tampered with, the signature verification fails and the token is rejected.
3. The core trade-off
The main difference between Session-Based Authentication and JWT Authentication.
1. Sessions (Stateful)

In session-based authentication, the server stores the user's login information in a session store such as Redis or a database. Every request contains a session ID, and the server looks up the session data before processing the request.
Advantages
["Users can be logged out immediately by deleting the session.","Permission changes take effect instantly because the server always reads the latest data from the session store."]
items: Users can be logged out immediately by deleting the session.
Permission changes take effect instantly because the server always reads the latest data from the session store.

blocks.content: Disadvantage
["All application servers need access to the same session store, creating a shared dependency."]
items: All application servers need access to the same session store, creating a shared dependency.

blocks.content: 2. Tokens (JWT) (Stateless)
In JWT authentication, the server does not store login information. The token itself contains the user's information and can be validated directly by any server.
Advantages
["Easy to scale horizontally because no shared session store is required.","Works well across microservices and different domains since any service can validate the token."]
items: Easy to scale horizontally because no shared session store is required.
Works well across microservices and different domains since any service can validate the token.

blocks.content: Disadvantage
["Revoking a token is difficult because it remains valid until it expires unless additional mechanisms such as blacklists are used."]
items: Revoking a token is difficult because it remains valid until it expires unless additional mechanisms such as blacklists are used.

blocks.content:
Note

The Core Trade-Off

Sessions provide better control and instant revocation, but require shared state.

JWT provides better scalability and simpler distributed architecture, but logout and permission changes are harder to handle immediately.

blocks.content: 4. Deep Dive: The Revocation Problem
The biggest practical difference between Sessions and JWT is how easily you can log a user out or invalidate their credentials.
With Sessions
Sessions are stored on the server, usually in Redis or a database. If a user logs out or an account is compromised, the server simply deletes the session record.
DELETE session:user123
The next request cannot find the session and immediately returns 401 Unauthorized.
Revocation is instant because the server controls the session data.
With JWT
JWTs are self-contained tokens. Once a token is issued, it remains valid until its expiration time (exp).
For example, if a JWT is valid for 24 hours and the account is compromised after 1 hour, the token can still be used for the remaining 23 hours.
You cannot simply "delete" a JWT because it is not stored on the server.
Solution 1: Short-Lived Access Tokens + Refresh Tokens
blocks.text: Solution 1: Short-Lived Access Tokens + Refresh Tokens

blocks.content: Use a short expiration for access tokens and a longer expiration for refresh tokens.

Access Token  → 15 minutes
Refresh Token → 30 days

Refresh Token → 30 days

This is the most common JWT approach.
Solution 2: Token Denylist
Store revoked token IDs (jti) in Redis.
revoked:token123 → true
Whenever a request arrives:
["Validate the JWT signature.","Check Redis to see if the token is revoked.","Reject the request if the token exists in the denylist."]

Check Redis to see if the token is revoked.
Reject the request if the token exists in the denylist.

blocks.content: This gives immediate revocation but adds some server-side state.
Solution 3: High-Security Systems
For banking or healthcare applications:
["Access tokens are very short-lived.","Refresh tokens are revoked immediately on suspicious activity."]
items: Access tokens are very short-lived.
Refresh tokens are revoked immediately on suspicious activity.

blocks.content: The user is effectively logged out within a few minutes without keeping full session state.
The Trade-Off
Sessions: Instant logout and easy revocation, but require shared storage.
JWT: Easy to scale and stateless, but revocation requires extra mechanisms like refresh tokens or token blacklists.
5. Token storage
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277447800-648925623.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart comparing where an access token can be stored on the client: localStorage and sessionStorage exposed to XSS versus an httpOnly cookie that JavaScript cannot read

blocks.content: The most dangerous part of token-based auth isn't the cryptography it's where the token is stored on the client.
1. localStorage
localStorage keeps data even after the browser is closed and reopened. Any JavaScript running on the page can read it.
localStorage.getItem("token");
The biggest problem is XSS attacks. If malicious JavaScript gets injected into your page, it can easily steal the token.
Use case: Generally avoid storing authentication tokens here.
2. sessionStorage
sessionStorage stores data only for the current browser tab. The data is deleted when the tab is closed.
sessionStorage.getItem("token");
It is slightly better than localStorage because the session does not survive browser restarts, but it is still accessible from JavaScript and therefore still vulnerable to XSS attacks.
Use case: Acceptable for temporary or short-lived sessions, but not ideal for authentication tokens.
3. httpOnly Cookie
An httpOnly cookie cannot be accessed by JavaScript.
The browser automatically sends the cookie with every request, but JavaScript cannot read or steal it.
The downside is that cookies need protection against CSRF attacks, usually by using SameSite=Strict, SameSite=Lax, or CSRF tokens.
Use case: Recommended for storing refresh tokens in most applications.

4. Recommended Approach
Access Token  → Store in memory
Refresh Token → Store in httpOnly cookie
blocks.text:
4. Recommended Approach
Access Token  → Store in memory
Refresh Token → Store in httpOnly cookie

blocks.content: The access token is used for API calls and disappears when the page refreshes or closes. The refresh token stays safely inside the httpOnly cookie and is used to obtain a new access token when needed.
This approach provides a good balance between security, user experience, and scalability.
6. Scaling
This is the most significant architectural difference when your system grows.
Session scaling problem:
You have 3 app servers. A user logs in to Server 1 and gets a session. Their next request goes to Server 2 (load balanced). Server 2 has no knowledge of the session created on Server 1.
1. Session Scaling

In session-based authentication, the user's session data is stored on the server. In a system with multiple application servers behind a load balancer, any request can go to any server. Therefore, all servers must be able to access the same session data.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277449435-149977954.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart of session scaling: a load balancer distributing requests across three app servers that all read and write to a shared Redis session store

blocks.content: To solve this, applications typically store sessions in a shared system like Redis. Every server reads and writes sessions from Redis, allowing any server to authenticate any user.
The downside is that sessions introduce shared state and an extra dependency. If the session store becomes unavailable, user authentication can fail across the entire system.
2. Token (JWT) Scaling
In JWT authentication, the server does not store any session data. The token itself contains the user's information and can be verified using a secret key or public key.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277451038-589062105.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart of JWT scaling: a load balancer distributing requests across three app servers that each verify the token locally with no shared session store

blocks.content: Because there is no shared state, every server can independently validate the token. Adding new servers, deploying in different regions, or running multiple microservices does not require session synchronization.
This makes JWT much easier to scale in distributed systems and microservice architectures because authentication becomes local, fast, and independent of a central session store.
The Core Difference: Sessions scale by sharing state through a central store like Redis. JWTs scale by eliminating shared state entirely, allowing every server to authenticate requests independently.
7. Access tokens and refresh tokens ( the production pattern )
blocks.text: 7. Access tokens and refresh tokens ( the production pattern )

blocks.content: No production system uses a single token that lasts 30 days. The standard pattern uses two tokens with very different characteristics.
1. Access Token
An access token is a short-lived token (usually 15 minutes) used for API requests.

["Sent in the Authorization: Bearer  header.","Proves that the user is authenticated.","Usually stored in memory (JavaScript variable).","If it gets stolen, the attacker can only use it for a short time."]
items: Sent in the Authorization: Bearer  header.
Proves that the user is authenticated.
Usually stored in memory (JavaScript variable).
If it gets stolen, the attacker can only use it for a short time.

blocks.content: Because access tokens are short-lived, we usually don't revoke them immediately and simply wait for them to expire.
2. Refresh Token
A refresh token is a long-lived token (typically 7–30 days).
["Stored in an httpOnly cookie.","Used only to get a new access token.","Stored on the server (database or Redis), so it can be revoked at any time."]
items: Stored in an httpOnly cookie.
Used only to get a new access token.
Stored on the server (database or Redis), so it can be revoked at any time.

blocks.content: If a user logs out or an account is compromised, the server simply deletes the refresh token.
Why Do We Need Both?: If we made the access token valid for 30 days, a stolen token would give an attacker access for an entire month.
Instead:
["Access token → short-lived and frequently expires.","Refresh token → long-lived and can be revoked."]
items: Access token → short-lived and frequently expires.
Refresh token → long-lived and can be revoked.

blocks.content: This gives both security and good user experience.
8. CSRF

Sessions stored in cookies are vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF). An attacker can create a malicious page that, when visited by a logged-in user, makes requests to your site using the user's session cookie (because cookies are sent automatically with cross-origin requests).
CSRF protection for sessions:

["SameSite=Strict: cookie attribute browser only sends the cookie for same-site requests. Cross-origin requests don't get the cookie. Modern browsers support this and it's the simplest protection.
","SameSite=La:cookie sent for same-site requests and top-level cross-site navigation (following a link). Not sent for sub-resource loads (img, script) from other sites. Good default for most applications.
","CSRF tokens: include a random token in each form, validate it server-side. The attacker can't read the CSRF token from your page (same-origin policy) so they can't include a valid one in their forged request.
"]
items: SameSite=Strict: cookie attribute browser only sends the cookie for same-site requests. Cross-origin requests don't get the cookie. Modern browsers support this and it's the simplest protection.

SameSite=La:cookie sent for same-site requests and top-level cross-site navigation (following a link). Not sent for sub-resource loads (img, script) from other sites. Good default for most applications.

CSRF tokens: include a random token in each form, validate it server-side. The attacker can't read the CSRF token from your page (same-origin policy) so they can't include a valid one in their forged request.

blocks.content: JWTs in Authorization headers are immune to CSRF. Because the JWT is in a JavaScript-accessible memory variable and sent via the Authorization: Bearer header, browsers don't automatically include it in cross-origin requests. CSRF only works against cookies. If you're using JWTs in headers, CSRF is not a concern.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 9. Comparing Both
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027811-381250843.png
blocks.alt: Diagram comparing session-based and token-based authentication side by side across state, revocation, and scaling

blocks.content: 10. The hybrid approach
The binary "sessions OR tokens" framing is a simplification. Most sophisticated applications use elements of both.

Refresh token stored server-side. The refresh token (which enables long-lived sessions) is stored in a database it's essentially a session record for the auth layer. When you revoke it, you delete the database record. The access token is still a stateless JWT, but the auth layer's persistence gives you session-like revocation control.

Access token in httpOnly cookie. Instead of storing the JWT in JavaScript memory (lost on page refresh) or localStorage (XSS risk), some architectures store it in an httpOnly cookie. The browser sends it automatically. JavaScript can't steal it via XSS. This is technically token-based but uses cookie transport like sessions combining the security of cookies with the statelessness of JWTs.

Session for the web app, JWT for the API. The web application uses traditional cookie-based sessions (easy, CSRF protection via SameSite, instant revocation). The mobile app and third-party integrations use JWTs (stateless, cross-domain, natural for non-browser clients). The backend auth layer issues both from the same authentication event.
When to choose which
Choose sessions when:

["Traditional web application, same domain, server-rendered pages","Instant revocation is a hard requirement (financial, healthcare, security-sensitive)","Simple architecture where a single Redis instance is not a burden","Users log in and stay logged in on one device","You control all clients and they're all browsers"]
items: Traditional web application, same domain, server-rendered pages
Instant revocation is a hard requirement (financial, healthcare, security-sensitive)
Simple architecture where a single Redis instance is not a burden
Users log in and stay logged in on one device
You control all clients and they're all browsers

blocks.content: Choose tokens when:

["API consumed by mobile apps, SPAs, or third-party clients","Microservices where multiple services need to verify identity without calling a central store","Cross-domain authentication (your API lives at api.example.com, your app at app.example.com)","Horizontal scaling where you don't want stateful dependencies","Third-party access via OAuth tokens are the natural mechanism for delegated access"]
items: API consumed by mobile apps, SPAs, or third-party clients
Microservices where multiple services need to verify identity without calling a central store
Cross-domain authentication (your API lives at api.example.com, your app at app.example.com)
Horizontal scaling where you don't want stateful dependencies
Third-party access via OAuth tokens are the natural mechanism for delegated access

blocks.content: The practical default for new systems today: JWT access tokens (15 min) + refresh tokens stored in the server's database (30 days) + refresh tokens sent via httpOnly cookies. This gives you most of the scalability benefits of stateless tokens while preserving the ability to revoke access within a short window. Both Shopify and GitHub use variations of this hybrid.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 11. HLD interview ( How to talk about this )
blocks.text: 11. HLD interview ( How to talk about this )

blocks.content: When designing any system with user authentication, the interviewer wants to see that you understand the trade-offs, not just the mechanisms.

Name the core distinction immediately. "Sessions are stateful the server stores session data and the client has a reference. Tokens are stateless the server stores nothing and the token itself carries the proof. The choice determines how you handle scaling, revocation, and cross-service identity."

Make a concrete recommendation with justification. "For this system a mobile API consumed by a React Native app I'd use JWTs. Mobile clients don't have a natural cookie jar, so sessions are awkward. JWTs in secure storage on the device are the standard. I'd issue short-lived access tokens (15 minutes) and a refresh token stored in the server's database for revocation control."

Address revocation proactively. "The main weakness of JWTs is revocation if a user's account is compromised, their access token remains valid until expiry. I'd handle this with a 15-minute access token lifetime plus a refresh token denylist in Redis. When we need to force-logout a user, we revoke the refresh token, and within 15 minutes their access token expires naturally. For sensitive actions password change, suspicious location I'd also check a token denylist."

Show you understand the scaling difference. "In a microservices architecture, sessions would require every service to call a central Redis to validate. With JWTs, each service verifies the token locally using the public key no network call. At scale this is significant: 200,000 requests per second to the auth service just to validate sessions is a real infrastructure cost. JWT verification is a sub-millisecond local operation."

Mention the hybrid if relevant. "In practice I'd use a hybrid: stateless JWT for access tokens (scales, no central store), but the refresh token is stored in a Postgres table server-side (gives us instant revocation of the long-lived credential). This is what most production auth implementations look like stateless where speed matters, stateful where revocation matters."

The depth that separates strong answers: knowing that the real engineering decision is not "sessions vs tokens" but specifically around revocation strategy, token lifetime, storage location, and how refresh tokens bridge the gap between stateless performance and stateful control.
